items.title: The religious beliefs of a hospital operator should not determine the healthcare available to Australians | Nisha Khot
items.summary:
Women suffer the consequences when Catholic healthcare providers acquire hospitals and create geographic deserts for abortion, contraception and IVF

In 2012 in Ireland, Dr Savita Halappanavar, who was then 17 weeks pregnant, attended a hospital with back pain. An examination found the pregnancy sac protruding through her womb. Her medical team refused to perform a procedure to end her pregnancy, because in Ireland the law prohibited abortion if a fetal heartbeat was still present. The 31-year-old developed sepsis and subsequently died of a cardiac arrest. During an inquest into her death, a midwife admitted to have said, “We don’t do that [abortion] here. Ireland is a Catholic country.” Halappanavar’s death became a catalyst for the campaign that ultimately led to the legalisation of abortion in Ireland.

This would never happen in Australia in 2026, I hear you say. Except, in Australia, Catholic hospitals provide healthcare based on the same Catholic beliefs as Irish hospitals did in 2012. And this scenario could very easily occur in Australia. In 2022, an ABC journalist interviewed an obstetrician working in an Australian Catholic hospital who described admitting a woman at 17 or 18 weeks whose waters had broken and a fetal heartbeat was still present. As the woman’s condition steadily deteriorated, the doctor was unable to recommend the care she required.
items.t: The religious beliefs of a hospital operator should not determine the healthcare available to Australians | Nisha Khot

items.summary:
Your Mileage May Vary is an advice column offering you a unique framework for thinking through your moral dilemmas. It’s based on value pluralism — the idea that each of us has multiple values that are equally valid but that often conflict with each other. To submit a question, fill out this anonymous form . Here’s this week’s question from a reader, condensed and edited for clarity: 

I’m considering moving my family from a red state to a blue state. I’ve lived in a red state my whole life, and as a lesbian with a wonderful trans wife, it is hard. Moving to a blue state could give my wife and I better nondiscrimination protections, better worker protections, and better access to health care. 

However, I feel like moving would be abandoning the good fight in my home state. I am well aware of how the red state exodus and the red state brain drain are already affecting our community. It’s hard to weigh what may be best for my wife against what’s best for our fellow red state residents. 

Dear Should I Stay or Should I Go,

I feel your question deep in my bones. Not long ago, I made the decision to move with my partner from the US to Canada, where I’m originally from. We’re also a queer couple. And we grappled with many of the same questions you’re wrestling with now.

Is it selfish to leave? If you leave, would you be putting your own family’s well-being above the well-being of your wider community? Does that mean you’re reneging on your values? 

A few key philosophical ideas really helped me navigate these questions, so I’ll walk you through them. Whether you agree or…

items.title: How America broke the turkey
items.summary:
Inside a farm that raises turkeys for Jennie-O, the second largest US turkey producer. | Photo courtesy of Kecia Doolittle 

Editor’s note, : This story was originally published on November 22, 2023, and reflects events that took place that year. We’re republishing it in its original form for this year’s Thanksgiving week. 

Late into the night on November 2, 2023, a few animal rights activists opened an unlocked barn door and stepped foot into a sea of turkeys living in gruesome conditions. It was one of several barns at a sprawling factory farming operation in Owatonna, Minnesota, that raises turkeys for Jennie-O, the country’s second-largest turkey producer and this year’s supplier to the annual White House turkey pardon ceremony. 

Inside this story 

An undercover investigation into one of America’s biggest turkey companies revealed sick birds in inhumane conditions. 

Part of the problem is the farms themselves, where turkeys are overcrowded and suffer from high rates of disease. 

But the biggest problem is the bird’s biology. To boost profits, turkey companies have bred turkeys to grow twice as fast, and nearly twice as big, as they were in the 1960s. 

The rapid growth causes a range of health issues, and many turkeys are so top-heavy they can hardly walk. 

“We documented a lot of really horrific health issues,” activist Kecia Doolittle, one of the investigators, told Vox. “It was about as bad as you can imagine.” 

They found numerous turkeys who were dead and rotting, Doolittle said, and many who had trouble walking. There were also live birds pecking at dead…
items.t: How America broke the turkey

items.title: Trump just can’t quit tariffs

President Donald Trump at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardoning ceremony at the White House on November 24, 2026. | Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images 

This story appeared in The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life. Subscribe here .

Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is trying to keep its trade war alive with new tariff announcements. 

Who’s getting tariffed? Potentially dozens of countries, including China, the EU’s 27 member states, South Korea, and others. If they take effect, the China tariffs would start at 20 percent and could escalate to as high as 40 percent, while EU tariffs would start at 15 percent and could go up from there.

How? Despite Wednesday’s announcement, it’s still not entirely clear when the new tariffs will take effect; according to the US trade adviser , Jamieson Greer, it’s unlikely to be sooner than “a couple months from now.” 

What’s the context? Courts have struck down two different attempts by the Trump administration to impose a global tariff regime, including the emergency authority the Supreme Court ruled on in February 2026.

Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland man who was wrongly deported and then indicted by the Trump administration, has left the US on his own terms, after more than a year of legal struggles that became emblematic of the administration’s often cruel and haphazard immigration policy. 

Abrego Garcia arrived in Madrid, Spain, on Wednesday, after choosing to “self-deport” to a country of his choice, rather than one of the African nations to which the Trump administration was trying to send him.

It’s the conclusion — for now — of a saga that began in March 2025, when Abrego Garcia was arrested by ICE and sent to an infamous megaprison in El Salvador. (Abrego Garcia is Salvadoran and does not have US citizenship, though he’s married to a US citizen.)

At the time of his deportation, ICE was legally barred from returning him to El Salvador because of threats to his life there. items.title: Why the Army detonated toxic explosives in Iowa
items.summary:
A sign identifying the facility sits inside a fence surrounding the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa, on November 19, 2026. | Scott Olson/Getty Images 

This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here .

On Wednesday, the Pentagon blew up about five tons of lead azide, an unstable explosive stored at an ammunition plant in Iowa, in order to dispose of it, sending a toxic plume of lead dust into the sky the day before Thanksgiving.

The detonation was briefly halted by a lower court before a federal circuit court cleared the way on Monday, and went forward despite serious public health concerns.

There was a real need for haste, according to the Army : The lead azide was sufficiently unstable that it was at risk of detonating on its own in an uncontrolled explosion, and falling temperatures in Iowa reportedly made such an explosion more likely. An uncontrolled explosion would have be more dangerous and unpredictable, and could have caused worse lead pollution.

At the same time, though, Iowa residents are angry and alarmed by a lack of clear information, poor communication by the Army, and the potential health hazards. 

The potential for things to go sideways had President Donald Trump nervous enough that he tried to pass the decision to Rob Sand — not the current Iowa governor, but the incoming Democratic governor-elect — and let any consequences fall on his head.

items.title: How to approach gifting so you don’t go broke, hurt anyone’s feelings, or end up drowning in crap
items.summary:
You don’t need me to tell you it’s expensive out there — groceries and gas cost a fortune, inflation is still hot hot hot , and getting a raise? Maybe next year, babe. 

If this is relatable for you, you might be dreading the holidays. Maybe not the celebrations, exactly, but the gift giving of it all — all the spending, all the stuff. Between the cost to your bank account and the cost to the planet, I wouldn’t blame you if the thought of holiday gifting was causing some angst right now. 

“The holidays are already stressful. Even if we think they’re fun, there’s a lot of stress associated with it,” financial therapist Lindsay Bryan-Podvin tells Vox. With higher prices on gas, groceries, travel, and eating out, “it’s compounding.”

It doesn’t have to be torturous, though. With the right approach, you can get your loved ones on board with a lower-cost, lower-waste holiday season. It just takes creativity and a little finesse.

Set your budget for gifts 

So, you know you want to do things differently this season but you’re still planning to do some gifting. The first step? Make a budget, Bryan-Podvin says.

A pro tip for next year 

Once you get through the chaos of this season, think about setting up a budget for gifting in January or February. 

Bryan-Podvin has a sinking fund called “Gifts” that she adds to every month. When a gifting occasion hits, she looks to that account to see how much she can afford to spend. 

“Whatever’s in there helps direct how much I will or won’t spend,” she says.

To set this up, see if your savings account offers a “bucketing” feature — a…
items.t: How to approach gifting so you don’t go broke, hurt anyone’s feelings, or end up drowning in crap

items.title: Stop eating turkey and start enjoying Thanksgiving
items.summary:
A turkey rescued from becoming meat is celebrated on Thanksgiving at the Gentle Barn animal sanctuary in California in 2025. | Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images 

I haven’t eaten turkey in many years, and a large share of Americans who have it on Thanksgiving would rather eat something else , too. That turkey is the most overrated part of this glorious long weekend between the end of summer and the winter holidays has become a cultural bit as familiar as the dead bird itself. As the journalist Brian McManus wrote for Vice : “It is, almost without fail, a dried-out, depressing hunk of sun-baked papier-mâché — a jaw-tiringly chewy, unsatisfying, and depressingly bland workout.”

“Throw it in the garbage,” The Guardian commanded about the Thanksgiving turkey a decade ago. That’s indeed what happens to many of them — perhaps their culinary mediocrity is part of why the equivalent of well over 8 million turkeys are thrown away as food waste on Thanksgiving.

This is all very strange, and sad, too, because life is too short to eat bad food on holidays — and the Thanksgiving turkey isn’t a mere harmless tradition. I know it’s untoward and uncool to talk about where our meat comes from at the holiday table, but putting millions of birds through hell for a dish many people can’t stop complaining about seems like a particularly concerning situation.

Turkeys are factory-farmed in the second-largest numbers of any animal in the US, after chickens. Most spend their short lives packed by the thousands into crowded sheds , where the stress can drive them to attack one…
items.t: Stop eating turkey and start enjoying Thanksgiving

items.title: The paradox of Latino ICE agents
items.summary:
Under the second Trump administration, immigration enforcement agencies have undergone a significant expansion. President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill raised ICE’s budget from $10 billion to $85 billion, making it the most funded law enforcement agency in the United States. With that funding, they began offering economic incentives like signing bonuses and student loan forgiveness programs. The number of ICE agents and officers doubled in just one year , with another recruiting push underway through the end of 2026. 

Today, perhaps more than ever, the front lines of those federal immigration law enforcement agencies reflect the demographics of the populations they were created to police. Latinos are overrepresented in the Department of Homeland Security , which houses ICE and Border Patrol. Self-identified Latinos account for nearly half of Border Patrol agents and about 30 percent of ICE agents .

So why do so many Latinos join the immigration enforcement agencies that have targeted their own communities? The answers reveal complexities about American Latino identity and the splintered points of view on immigration policy at the border. 

Hosted by Kahlil Greene , this video is part of our new series, Kahlil Explains, that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society. This episode traces the evolution of immigration enforcement agencies and their appeal to Latino recruits, to explain why so many ICE and Border Patrol agents are Latino. 

Read and watch more about the Latino community and…
items.t: The paradox of Latino ICE agents

items.title: Buy now, pay later is more dangerous than ever
items.summary:
An unsettling thing happens almost any time you buy something these days. You get to the checkout page and there’s an offer: Would you like to split this purchase up into four easy interest-free payments? 

Parting with a smaller amount of money to get something you want sooner is a compelling offer. So compelling that nearly 40 percent shoppers in the United States plan to use “buy now, pay later” (BNPL) services for holiday shopping this year , according to a NerdWallet survey. The same percentage of people said they don’t expect to make payments in full or on-time. Another survey showed that half of millennials and Gen Z prefer payment options like Affirm and Klarna to credit cards and more than half rely on BNPL for items they can’t afford. These are the same young people who are having a hard time finding a job , struggling to pay overdue student loan bills , and dealing with rising food prices . That might be why it felt so dark when DoorDash announced a partnership with Klarna in 2025, ushering in an era where people are taking out loans to pay for their takeout. 

As affordability remains the dominant issue in American politics , the holiday shopping season feels different this year. Everything is more expensive, sure. But with BNPL options being offered by everyone from fintech startups to major banks, it’s also easier than ever to finance purchases you couldn’t otherwise afford. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has taken some of the guardrails off this shadowy lending industry, leaving consumers more vulnerable to unexpected fees and endless debt. Some are…
items.t: Buy now, pay later is more dangerous than ever

items.title: A few questions for the guy who went snorkeling in a Home Depot retention pond
items.summary:
Joseph Ricketts in the retention pond. | Joseph Ricketts 

One night earlier this fall, a biologist and YouTuber in Florida named Joseph Ricketts went snorkeling in a retention pond next to his local Home Depot. 

He filmed what he saw and posted a video to his channel titled “ Night Snorkel In a Home Depot Retention Pond .” It quickly blew up, hitting more than 2 million views as of this writing, and for good reason: It’s not at all what you might expect.

Ricketts found an aquatic world teeming with life on his dive into what is, from the surface, a stagnant pool of water filled with old beer cans. A water snake undulated through the pond, a bulge in its stomach revealing a recent meal. Tadpoles darted about, some of them half on their way to froghood. Mysterious shrimp scuttled along the silty bottom.

Ricketts, who works as a crocodile and alligator research biologist in Florida, went for his first snorkeling trip when he was 16 years old. On that trip, he came face-to-face with a manatee — and was instantly hooked. “I experienced so much joy in that moment, and I just kind of subconsciously knew I’d be chasing that for the rest of my life to some degree or another,” he told me. 

Ricketts still takes a lot of joy in snorkeling, in part because of how it allows him to quickly access a totally different world hiding just under the surface of the water; his YouTube bio declares, “I’ll snorkel pretty much anywhere.” And his recent retention pond dive among the suburban detritus bears that out. 

I talked with Ricketts recently about urban ecology, snorkeling, and what…

items.title: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar
items.summary:
By nine votes to six, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in connection with its 2017 “clearance operations” in Rakhine State. The ruling is an alarm bell for all states accused of genocide.

The year 2017 was not the first Rohingya exodus from Myanmar: in 1978 and again in 1991-92, hundreds of thousands of Rohingya poured into Bangladesh to escape state persecution. Many returned, and were forced to flee again when new violence erupted.

Today, more than 1.2 million Rohingya are in refugee camps in Bangladesh without any concrete prospect to return to Myanmar. Most Rohingya want to return, but not without conditions that would ensure their safety. The most crucial condition is the guarantee of citizenship rights.

Since Myanmar stripped the Rohingya of their citizenship in 1982, they have been living under apartheid-like conditions. Among many discriminatory policies imposed on Rohingya life,…
items.t: Justice is elusive for the Rohingya even after the ICJ’s landmark genocide ruling against Myanmar

items.title: Mother tongue language rights don’t implement themselves: Lessons from Nepal’s classrooms
items.summary:
In a Grade 2 classroom in Rautahat, in Nepal’s southern plains, teacher Renuka Dahal holds up a picture card of a mango. She gives the Nepali word, then asks her students what they call it at home. They respond in Tharu and Maithili, the languages many of them speak with their families.

“I ask my students to teach me words in their language,” she told UNICEF in 2025. “It makes them feel that I care about who they are.” And that small exchange marks a real change.

For Canadians interested in Indigenous language revitalization, and for teachers welcoming newcomer students, Nepal’s experience shows what it takes to move language rights off paper and into the classroom.

For generations, many children in Nepal started school in a language they didn’t understand. Yet research shows that beginning school in a familiar language can strengthen learning and make it easier to acquire additional languages, including Nepali and English.

Nepal has written that lesson into its 2015 Constitution, which guarantees communities the right to education in their mother tongue.

items.summary:
The recent failure of the UN climate summit, Cop31, went beyond already gloomy expectations. Yet this political and diplomatic catastrophe may become a historical opportunity for global climate governance to tackle its structural problems.

It is a miracle that Cop climate summits have survived and grown for 31 years, with all decisions needing unanimous consensus from all 195 nations or parties. Cops have produced some positive results such as the 2015 Paris climate agreement to cut greenhouse gases. But now it’s time for radical reform. A reform that must not only abolish unanimity, but also make the Cop capable of engaging a strong enough coalition of interests to advance the climate change agenda.

items.title: Let’s hear it for the leftwing echo chamber | Zoe Williams
items.summary:
By chance, I found myself committed to a debate with people whose views I share. It was an eye-opening experience

I was on a panel recently in a church – St Luke’s in Battersea, south London – about the future of the welfare state, except the other panellists booked to speak on the right of politics were unwell and couldn’t come. And so we ended up with an entirely leftwing panel (albeit different shades of the left).

Puckishly, I suggested that I would split my six minutes of allocated speaking time and do three on what the rightwing panellists would have said, had they appeared, and then three on why they are wrong. But I couldn’t get the arguments right. I know they think the current welfare bill is – between our ageing population, our Neets and our dated expectations about what a decent life looks like and whose job it is to ensure you have one – “unsustainable”. I just couldn’t summon the right mix of tough-minded realism and benign resignation to other people’s misery. It wouldn’t come out of my mouth.

items.title: It’s time for scientists to boycott the climate COPs and the IPCC
items.summary:
On Nov. 22, the day after COP31 climate talks collapsed in Antalya, Turkey, the global average temperature at noon UTC was estimated to be a record-setting 2.36 C above the pre-industrial average.

Climate change is driving up global temperatures. Yet governments could not even agree to name the fossil fuels driving it.

I have been a climate scientist since the late 1980s and have followed every UN climate summit since the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro. I cannot recall a more embarrassing failure than COP31.

The first draft proposed at least US$120 billion by 2035 to help countries adapt to climate change. By Nov. 19, the figure was gone.

Three years ago in Dubai, governments agreed to transition away from fossil fuels. The Nov. 16 Antalya draft said so plainly. Yet, the final proposal at COP31 still omitted any mention of fossil fuels. The European Union and small island states were right to reject it.

Given the recent failure, is it time for scientists and activists to boycott COP?

items.t: It’s time for scientists to boycott the climate COPs and the IPCC

items.title: PNG’s parliament is voting on ratifying Bougainville independence. A ‘no’ won’t be the end of the story
items.summary:
After more than a century of struggle, Bougainville is moving closer to becoming the world’s newest nation. An autonomous region of Papua New Guinea (PNG) in the northern Solomon Islands chain, Bougainville is taking its next step toward self-determination after a decade-long civil war and a 25-year peace process.

In a 2019 referendum, almost 98% of Bougainvilleans voted for independence. Today the parliament of PNG will begin to vote on ratifying that result.

A “yes” vote in parliament, if it comes, won’t immediately make Bougainville independent. But it will set the legal machinery moving.

Hard questions such as the future of the island’s contentious Panguna mine remain unresolved, but the vote offers a chance to recognise decades of work from the Bougainvillean and PNG sides that have kept the peace process on track.
